prs.title: Fix `token_expiry_time` upon context initialization for stored tokens.
prs.author: keurcien
prs.reason: [llm] cluster primary: After tokens are loaded from persistent storage, `token_expiry_time` is never (re)computed. `is_token_valid()` therefore treats a stale/expired token as still valid, so the proactive-refresh path is skipped and the client falls through to a full interactive re-authorization instead of a silent refresh on restart. (2 PRs)
prs.short_reason: [llm] cluster primary: After tokens are loaded from persistent storage, `token_expiry_time` is never (re)computed. `is_token_valid()` therefore treats a stale/expired token as still valid, so the proactive-refresh path is skipped and the client falls through to a full interactive re-authorization instead of a silent refresh on restart. (2 PRs)
prs.cluster_pick_reason: #1784 fixes the actual root cause: it calls context.update_token_expiry() inside _initialize() whenever a stored token has expires_in set, so token_expiry_time is correct for every consumer of is_token_valid() (both the proactive pre-request check and the reactive 401 handler), with a 4-line core change plus a dedicated expired_tokens test fixture. #2875's own inline comment names this exact bug ('a provider reloaded from storage never restores token_expiry_time') but only patches the symptom by adding a stored-refresh-token fallback inside the 401 branch of async_auth_flow (~15 added lines of control flow); it leaves token_expiry_time itself wrong, so any other code path that relies on is_token_valid() remains affected.

prs.short_reason: [llm] cluster primary: Both patch the exact same conditional in FuncMetadata.pre_parse_json (`isinstance(data_value, str) and field_info.annotation is not str`) to stop the function from JSON-decoding string values whose declared type is a union that includes `str`, which corrupts plain strings that happen to look like JSON (e.g. "null", "123", "{...}"). prs.title: fix: buffer stdio server writes during progress notifications
prs.reason: [llm] cluster primary: Both change the hardcoded 0-capacity memory object stream used for write_stream in stdio_server, targeting the same root cause: a zero-capacity write stream forces the writer task to rendezvous on every send, which stalls when a handler needs to queue a final response while stdout_writer is still flushing an earlier message (e.g. a progress notification). #2215 exposes read_stream_buffer_size/write_stream_buffer_size as caller-supplied parameters (default 0, i.e. unchanged behavior unless a caller opts in). #2654 instead hardcodes write_stream's capacity to 1 so the fix applies by default, and adds a BlockingStdout-based regression test that reproduces the progress-notification stall. (2 PRs)
prs.short_reason: [llm] cluster primary: Both change the hardcoded 0-capacity memory object stream used for write_stream in stdio_server, targeting the same root cause: a zero-capacity write stream forces the writer task to rendezvous on every send, which stalls when a handler needs to queue a final response while stdout_writer is still flushing an earlier message (e.g. a progress notification). #2215 exposes read_stream_buffer_size/write_stream_buffer_size as caller-supplied parameters (default 0, i.e. unchanged behavior unless a caller opts in). #2654 instead hardcodes write_stream's capacity to 1 so the fix applies by default, and adds a BlockingStdout-based regression test that reproduces the progress-notification stall. (2 PRs)
prs.cluster_pick_reason: Fixes the stall by default (write buffer size 1) rather than requiring every caller to discover and pass a new parameter — #2215's default of 0 leaves the bug present unless a caller opts in. #2654 also ships a targeted regression test (BlockingStdout) reproducing the exact progress-notification stall, whereas #2215's test changes are incidental to the signature change. Both edit the same create_context_streams call for write_stream and conflict; #2215's configurability could still be layered on top of #2654's default later if wanted.

members.title: fix(stdio): allow configurable memory stream buffer size
members.author: yaowubarbara
members.reason: [llm] duplicates #2654: Both change the hardcoded 0-capacity memory object stream used for write_stream in stdio_server, targeting the same root cause: a zero-capacity write stream forces the writer task to rendezvous on every send, which stalls when a handler needs to queue a final response while stdout_writer is still flushing an earlier message (e.g. a progress notification). #2215 exposes read_stream_buffer_size/write_stream_buffer_size as caller-supplied parameters (default 0, i.e. unchanged behavior unless a caller opts in). #2654 instead hardcodes write_stream's capacity to 1 so the fix applies by default, and adds a BlockingStdout-based regression test that reproduces the progress-notification stall.
